# Tooling as of October 2026 {#sec-tooling}

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this appendix exists

This appendix is dated, and it is meant to be replaced. It holds
the perishable half of @sec-ai-coding: the `ellmer` interface for
calling a model from R, the model identifier, the names of the
coding agents in common use, and the `btw` and Model Context
Protocol (MCP) setup, each as it stood in October 2026. Package
interfaces, product names, and model identifiers change on a
schedule of months. The chapter therefore keeps the durable
practice (the four Cs, the failure modes, governance, and
provenance) and sends the reader here for the commands. When the
commands below stop working, rewrite this appendix against the
current documentation. Nothing in the chapter should need to
change.
:::

## Models and agents from R {#sec-ai-tooling}

Everything in this section is perishable. @sec-ai-coding does
not depend on it, and every rule of @sec-ai-governance applies to
each tool below.

### Calling a model from R with `ellmer`

`ellmer` [@wickham2026ellmer], from Posit, provides an R interface
to LLM APIs (application programming interfaces). A prompt in a
script can be put under version control, whereas a copy-paste
from a chat window cannot. An LLM call can sit inside an R
function that takes input from your pipeline and returns output
to it. In addition, `ellmer` supports tool use (the model calls R
functions you provide), structured output (validated against a
schema), and streaming. The following is display-only, because it
needs an API key:

```r
install.packages("ellmer")
library(ellmer)

# model identifiers are retired on a schedule: this one was current
# as of October 2026; models_anthropic() lists what is available now
model_id <- "claude-opus-5-5"
chat <- chat_anthropic(model = model_id)
# or chat_openai(), chat_google_gemini(), chat_ollama() for local

chat$chat("Translate this regex to plain English: '^\\d{3}-\\d{2}-\\d{4}$'")
chat$chat("What about variants with no separator?")

# stream() returns a generator, consumed chunk by chunk
stream <- chat$stream("Long analysis...")
coro::loop(for (chunk in stream) cat(chunk))
```

Older code and tutorials call `chat_claude()`. Current `ellmer`
names the function `chat_anthropic()`, after the provider rather
than the model family. Keep the model identifier in one variable,
as here, and record its value alongside your results. A script
that names a retired model stops running, and a result produced by
an unrecorded model cannot be reproduced.

Set the API key once, in a project-local `.Renviron` that is listed
in `.gitignore` and never committed (display-only):

```bash
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=<your key>
OPENAI_API_KEY=<your key>
```

Restart R, and `ellmer` reads the variables automatically.

A short worked example: a function that asks a model to explain
another function and list its unhandled edge cases (display-only).

```r
explain_function <- function(fn, model_id) {
  prompt <- paste0(
    "Explain in one paragraph what this R function does, ",
    "and identify any bugs or edge cases it does not handle:\n\n",
    paste(deparse(fn), collapse = "\n")
  )
  chat <- chat_anthropic(model = model_id)
  chat$chat(prompt)
}

explain_function(function(x) {
  x |> filter(!is.na(value)) |> summarize(mean = mean(value))
}, model_id = model_id)
```

The function sends code, not data. Its output is a starting point
for review, checked against your own reading.

### Coding agents

An interactive coding agent gives the model direct file-edit and
shell access. That is, it reads files, makes targeted edits, runs
the tests, and iterates on the output. As of October 2026 the
common ones in the terminal (CLI, command-line interface) are
Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and GitHub Copilot CLI. In the
IDE (integrated development environment) they are Cursor and
Positron Assistant. An agent is suited to multi-file refactors
where the model needs the whole project. It is also suited to
iterative debugging where the model needs to run the code and
observe failures, and to large tasks where copy-paste would be
tedious. Use a chat window for quick lookups, and write the code
yourself where you want control of every edit. An agent is more
capable and more dangerous than a chat window, and every rule in
@sec-ai-governance applies to it.

### Live documentation with `btw`

The `btw` package gives a model the documentation of your
installed packages and a view of the R session. It does this
either by copying that context for a chat window or as an MCP
server that an agent calls. As of October 2026 the setup is as
follows. It is display-only; check the package README, because
these interfaces change.

```r
install.packages("btw")
btw::btw("{dplyr}", "?dplyr::left_join", trial)
```

```bash
claude mcp add -s user r-btw -- Rscript -e "btw::btw_mcp_server()"
```

The first call gathers a package overview, a help page, and a
description of a data frame for pasting into a chat. The second
registers `btw`'s MCP server with Claude Code; other agents have
equivalent commands. A description of a data frame includes
values from it, so the governance rules apply to what `btw` sends.
Point it at synthetic data.

### Exercises

1. Write a function of under 20 lines that uses
   `chat_anthropic()` to summarize a block of R code passed as a
   string, with the model identifier as an argument and the
   provenance (model, date) attached to the result.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```r
summarize_code <- function(code, model_id) {
  chat <- ellmer::chat_anthropic(model = model_id)
  reply <- chat$chat(paste0(
    "Summarize what this R code does in three sentences. ",
    "Do not suggest changes.\n\n", code
  ))
  structure(reply, model = model_id, date = Sys.Date())
}
```

The identifier is an argument rather than a string inside the
function, so it is set and recorded in one place. The attributes
carry the provenance with the result. The function sends code
only; pass it nothing that contains data.
:::

### The LLM-evaluation harness, as of October 2026 {#sec-tooling-eval}

@sec-ai-eval describes the durable idea. Before an LLM step runs
unsupervised on a column of data, build a labeled validation set,
score the step against it, and decide a threshold before you see
the number. The code that implements that idea belongs in this
appendix, because the function names on an LLM client change
faster than the practice does. The script below is complete
enough to run as written, given an API key and the packages
installed. The HF-HOME `med_text` example is the one
@sec-ai-eval walks through by hand.

```r
# R/eval_med_frequency.R
library(ellmer)
library(dplyr)

#' Classify one dosing string's frequency with a structured LLM call
#' @param med_text character scalar, a `medications.csv` dosing string
#' @param model_id character scalar, an `ellmer`-supported model
#'   identifier (current as of October 2026; see models_anthropic())
#' @return one of "once daily", "twice daily", "as needed", "other"
classify_frequency <- function(med_text, model_id) {
  chat <- chat_anthropic(model = model_id, system_prompt = paste(
    "You classify a medication dosing instruction by frequency.",
    "Answer with exactly one category."
  ))
  chat$extract_data(
    paste("Dosing instruction:", med_text),
    type = type_enum(c("once daily", "twice daily",
                       "as needed", "other"))
  )
}

#' Score a labeled validation set against the classifier
#' @param val_set data frame with columns `med_text`, `label`
#' @param model_id passed to classify_frequency()
#' @return val_set with a `predicted` column, plus printed accuracy
#'   and a confusion matrix, as a side effect
run_eval <- function(val_set, model_id) {
  val_set$predicted <- vapply(val_set$med_text, classify_frequency,
                              character(1), model_id = model_id)
  accuracy <- mean(val_set$predicted == val_set$label)
  confusion <- table(predicted = val_set$predicted,
                     true = val_set$label)
  log_line <- sprintf(
    "%s | model=%s | n=%d | accuracy=%.3f",
    Sys.Date(), model_id, nrow(val_set), accuracy)
  cat(log_line, "\n", file = "eval-log.txt", append = TRUE)
  list(val_set = val_set, accuracy = accuracy, confusion = confusion,
       log_line = log_line)
}

val_set <- read.csv("validation/med-frequency-labels.csv",
                    colClasses = "character")
result <- run_eval(val_set, model_id = "claude-opus-5-5")
result$accuracy
result$confusion

stopifnot(result$accuracy >= 0.90)
```

Three choices in this script are each a place where a
reasonable-looking first draft goes wrong.

First, the model identifier is a parameter instead of a literal
buried in the classifier function. `run_eval()` takes `model_id`
and writes it into the log line alongside the date and the
accuracy. Eventually the identifier is retired, as
@sec-ai-tooling's warning about `ellmer`'s model lifecycle
describes. When that happens, the log shows exactly which accuracy
number belongs to which model. Re-running the harness against the
replacement is then a one-line change at the call site, not a
search through the codebase for a hard-coded string.

Second, the threshold is enforced by a `stopifnot()` instead of
stated in a comment. Here `accuracy >= 0.90` is a number chosen
for illustration. In a real project it is the number decided in
advance, following @sec-ai-eval's point about deciding the bar
before seeing the result. The script then fails loudly when the
bar is missed. This is the same discipline @sec-testing-ci
applies to a test suite's exit status, and it keeps a
disappointing validation run from being quietly accepted.

Third, the log is appended to, never overwritten.
`eval-log.txt` accumulates one line per run. A later reader
(including the harness's own author) can then see the accuracy
trend across model and prompt changes rather than only the most
recent number. Commit this log alongside the code. This is the
same provenance habit @sec-ai-practice teaches for a single
generated function, extended to a step that runs many times.

Some projects will want the dataset-solver-scorer structure built
for them rather than written by hand as above. For those, `vitals`
[@couch2026vitals] expresses the same harness as a `Task`. The
code is display-only and current as of October 2026; check the
package's own vignette for the exact interface before relying on
it.

```r
library(vitals)

freq_task <- Task$new(
  dataset = val_set,                  # columns: input, target
  solver  = generate(),               # calls the model under test
  scorer  = model_graded_qa()         # or an exact-match scorer
)
freq_task$eval(model = "claude-opus-5-5", epochs = 1)
```

`vitals` writes its evaluation log in the same format Inspect uses.
This is useful mainly if you expect to outgrow R for this task and
want a log format the Python tooling can read. For a single column
of a single compendium, the hand-written harness above is often
the simpler choice. It is also the one that needs no further
package to be understood.
